title: Using a vessel mask as a hint to tell arteries from veins in eye scans
paper_title: RavNet: Conditioning Retinal Vessel Identification Using a Cascaded Multi-objective U-Net
date_note: COMSYS 2024 (5th Int. Conf. on Frontiers in Computing and Systems), BITS Pilani Goa campus, 13-15 Dec 2024; Springer volume published 2025
venue: 5th International Conference on Frontiers in Computing and Systems (COMSYS 2024)
summary: RavNet uses two U-Nets in a row. The first finds where the vessels are, and the second uses that map to label arteries and veins separately in infrared scans of the retina.

body.p: The retina is the only deep micro-vessel bed that can be seen directly, without surgery or injury. That makes it useful for diagnosing systemic disorders such as diabetes, high blood pressure and leukemia. We built RavNet, a pair of neural networks that first finds all the vessels in an infrared eye scan and then uses that result to mark arteries and veins separately.

The retinal vessels work as a window into the body's smallest blood circulation. Changes in them, such as narrowing or leakage, can point to disease. Marking each pixel of a scan as artery, vein or background is called segmentation. Accurate segmentation can feed automated diagnostic tools, which the paper says could be deployed in remote or underserved areas for early screening without a specialist.

We worked with the RAVIR dataset. It holds 46 infrared images taken with a scanning laser ophthalmoscope, a device that sweeps a laser over the retina. The images come from the UCLA Stein Eye Institute and have high quality and high contrast. To enlarge the training data we applied horizontal flips, vertical flips and rotations.

The standard tool for this job is the U-Net. It is shaped like the letter U. An encoder shrinks the image step by step to capture what is in it, and a decoder expands it back to a full-size label map. Shortcuts called skip connections help the decoder recover the full spatial resolution at the output.

RavNet runs two U-Nets in sequence. The first only produces a binary mask: vessel or no vessel. We then stack that mask with the original scan and give both to a second network, so that it starts with a prediction of where the vessels are.

figure.alt: Pipeline diagram: an eye scan goes through a first encoder-decoder to give a binary vessel mask; the scan and mask are stacked and fed to a second encoder that feeds an artery decoder, a vein decoder and an image-reconstruction decoder.
figure.caption: The cascade. The first network makes a vessel mask. The second network gets the scan plus that mask and has three decoders.

body.p: The second network has one encoder and three decoders. One decoder outputs arteries and one outputs veins. The third, labelled the regularizer in the figure, rebuilds the input scan. This extra task serves to regularize the outputs, which means it acts as a constraint that guides training.

Both networks use residual blocks, dropout and batch normalization, and the encoder works at six resolutions. For training, the vessel pixels get a larger weight of 0.75 in the cross-entropy loss, because they are of greater importance. We used binary cross-entropy together with Dice loss for the vessel outputs and mean squared error for the reconstruction. The Dice measure is twice the overlap of the true and predicted masks divided by the sum of their areas.

We evaluated RavNet on unseen retinal scans and compared it with four U-Net-based models: U-Net, Dense U-Net, Residual U-Net and R2U-Net. It had the highest Dice score for both vessel types. For arteries, RavNet reached 0.7790, against 0.7510 for the plain U-Net and 0.7621 for R2U-Net (Table 1). For veins it reached 0.7890, against 0.7674 for the U-Net and 0.7826 for R2U-Net (Table 2). The paper concludes that RavNet outperforms the U-Net-based models it was compared with.

body.callout: Dice scores: 0.7790 for arteries and 0.7890 for veins, the highest among the five models compared.

figure.caption: Four example scans. From left: the original image, the original mask, and RavNet's artery and vein extractions.

body.p: RavNet is not ahead on every measure. For veins it had the highest specificity (0.9929) but the lowest sensitivity of the five models (0.7385), so it detects fewer of the true vein pixels (Table 2). For arteries, R2U-Net had a slightly higher accuracy, 0.9706 against 0.9701 (Table 1). The dataset is small, only 46 images. The paper lists stronger data augmentation, multimodal imaging, real-time use, transfer learning and clinical validation as future work.

According to the abstract, the improvement in vessel delineation comes from incorporating the mask predictions of the first model. The longer-term aim is the kind of screening tool for remote or underserved areas mentioned above.
